newsitem.title: ALBANIA: EU military experts scout Albania amid violence.
newsitem.headline: EU military experts scout Albania amid violence.

text.p: Military experts from European Union countries scouted Albania on Wednesday to prepare for a possible multinational aid protection force in the troubled Balkan state, still racked by random violence.
"The team is made up of experts from all fields which could be involved in any kind of military operation," an EU diplomat, who requested anonymity, said.
The team will stay for several days and includes military experts from the Florence-based Eurofor force - Italy, France, Portugal and Spain - as well as Austrian and Greek personnel.
Albania has appealed for a multinational force to oversee relief operations and to help reestablish order after weeks of violence and an insurrection which has cut the country in two.

In Vienna, the 54-member Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) was close to agreeing on a framework for a broad international military force, made up of volunteer nations, diplomatic sources said.
Armed rebels and lawless gangs control most of the south from Vlore, on the Adriatic coast, to the Greek border. Theft, violence and settling of scores has become daily fare.
A Dutch journalist was shot on Tuesday in the southern port of Sarande. She was in hospital on the nearby Greek island of Corfu.
Wilma Goudappel worked with several Western media groups and had run a Sarande hotel for several years. It was unclear whether she was shot for her media work or some other reason.

Masked men in Vlore forced four Italian doctors at gunpoint to evacuate a wounded comrade on Tuesday. The doctors left by helicopter with the wounded man just two days after arriving to work with an Italian Red Cross relief mission in Vlore.

Three policemen were shot dead on Monday in the town, which has seen some of the worst violence in a popular uprising which toppled one government and is posing President Sali Berisha with his worse crisis since coming to power in 1992.
Vlore remains lawless and 24 people wounded in recent weeks have been taken to Greece in convoys of private cars over the past two days for treatment.

"I don't know what else to do. I have no means to protect these people," police chief Milto Kordha told Reuters. He noted the government had sent armoured personnel carriers to ensure order in Fier, just to the north, but none to Vlore.

The state-run ATA news agency reported that in the southern town of Berat a 17-year-old boy was tied to a tree, doused with petrol and set ablaze. It said 42 people had been killed in the town and surrounding villages since the uprising began.
Albania has been swept by violence since January when a series of popular but fraudulent investment schemes collapsed wiping out millions of dollars in savings.
Riots and protests against the schemes were followed by a popular uprising in the south with thousands of people seizing weapons from army depots and setting up rebel councils.
Most southern towns are still in revolt against Berisha, demanding that he quit before they surrender their guns. But the region has also been swept by violence from armed gangs.
Berisha clung to power by sacking his rightist Democratic Party government and replacing it this month with a national unity cabinet headed by opposition socialist Bashkim Fino.
He agreed to elections by June and said he would quit if his party lost but he has expressed some optimism recently as he sought help from the European Union and other groups.
"I am fully convinced that I have my supporters in the south. There is a great silent majority," he was quoted as saying in an interview with the Times of London newspaper.
In another interview, he said that slow progress was being made on reestablishing order and disarming thousands of people who have stolen guns from the army.

"Order is being progressively reestablished. There is a slight improvement but the disarming process cannot be swift," to told the French daily Le Monde. "There is a very special relationship between Albanians and their rifles. We are a warlike country and one has to be patient."
Part of his patience stems from the disintegration of the army and police forces during the popular uprising. He has no force at the moment to send against the southern rebels.
A new EU mission will visit Albania on Wednesday to work out how to help. The 10-member EU delegation, the second in two weeks, will meet Fino and other ministers.
